chapter: Writing, Oklahoma roots and the origins of bebop
title: How McGhee learned to write
summary: Writing meant relying on piano and on knowing brass and reeds, with Armstrong and Eldridge as influences.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I think I left off when we were talking about how I learned how to write music.

It is a beautiful thing to learn how to write, and very few people that I hear that have a distinctive thing about their own music that they don't be copying somebody -- they'll be copying someone one way, shape, form or another. But it's a beautiful thing to hear somebody write something, or write something that ain't even pretty but it's original. It's kind of hard to find somebody that can do that. And I find it very hard for myself just to sit down and write an original score without really reflecting back on some of the things that I've heard or some of the things that I've heard people play, or the mood of the tune or whatever... It's something that has been used in some way, shape, form or another.
Well, you have to start someplace...
Now, when you started, you really didn't start by listening to records and picking up on somebody originally, did you?
Well, no. No more than Louis Armstrong and Roy Eldridge. I always listened to them.
But you were listening to them as soloists.
Yeah, I was listening to them as Jazz players.
But what about your writing, when you started to write?

Well, then, I had to use the material that I had, within my knowledge, to write out something that would sound good. And I was lucky. I found out, knowing brass and the reeds, I could get a better idea of how I wanted them to sound than any other way.
Now, in those days, and I'm talking back in Oklahoma and New Mexico...
That's what I'm talking about, yeah.
Did you go to the piano to write?

Yeah, I had to keep going to the piano. That was the most mysterious thing in my life, I think, was the piano. Like, right now, I have to go the piano to find out just exactly where I'm at, and from there I can go on to other things. But you've got to get to that piano. That's a very definite must.
Also, once you first heard your arrangements played, then did you get an idea of how to do the next thing?
